target: AG1's claim that real animal dissection is educationally superior and ethically acceptable because most dissected animals were already dead or were byproducts
objection: Animal dissection is not uniquely necessary for learning, because synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same anatomy and lab skills, and the usual supply chains for dissection animals are harmful and environmentally damaging; therefore the practice is unjustified.

target: AG2's claim that dissection animals typically come from harmful wild-capture supply chains and that this makes the practice unethical
objection: That supply-chain picture does not match many school dissections: according to the opposing side's cited reality in classroom contexts, over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased and fetal pigs are often meat-industry byproducts, so the wild-capture/biodiversity-harm objection is not the normal classroom case.

target: AG1's claim that using already-dead animals makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Even if some specimens are already dead, that does not erase the harm involved in obtaining dissection animals; the broader supply chain commonly involves wild capture, which reduces local populations and biodiversity, so the practice remains ethically and environmentally wrong.

target: AG2's claim that non-animal alternatives can provide the same educational and skill value as real dissection
objection: Models and simulations do not fully replace real dissection, because handling real tissues uniquely develops deeper three-dimensional anatomical understanding and practical lab skills such as fine motor control and hand-eye coordination through tactile interaction with actual organs and tissues.

target: AG1's claim that real dissection has unique educational and skill benefits
objection: Well-designed synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same anatomy and help students build lab-relevant skills, often more consistently than variable real specimens, so real animal dissection is not necessary for the stated educational outcomes.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives can teach the same relationships and skills as real dissection
objection: The assumption that models and simulations fully substitute for real dissection is not supported, because only real dissection provides tactile experience with authentic tissue, biological variability, and the psychomotor practice of manipulating real organs and structures.

target: AG1's claim that dissection also helps inspire science careers and provides 'aha' moments
objection: Career inspiration and 'aha' moments are not unique to animal dissection, because the same motivational effects can come from simulations, models, microscopy, and other non-lethal biology activities.

target: AG2's claim that classroom dissection usually depends on harmful wild-capture supply chains
objection: That premise is wrong for many school programs: most specimens are already deceased, and fetal pigs are commonly meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so wild-capture is not the governing reality of typical classroom dissection.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is educationally worthwhile even if not required by standards or medical training
objection: If AP Biology, NGSS, and medical training do not require animal dissection, then it is an unnecessary activity, and an unnecessary harmful activity should not be permitted when alternatives exist.

target: AG2's claim that real dissection is unnecessary because standards and medical training do not require it
objection: Educational value does not depend on strict curricular or physician-training requirements; real dissection still provides unique embodied learning, practical lab skills, and ethical acceptability when specimens are already dead or byproducts.

target: AG1's claim that real dissection uniquely develops deep understanding and hands-on skills
objection: Those learning goals are about recognizing anatomy, interpreting structures, and practicing manipulation, and well-designed models or simulations can deliver those same outcomes without using dead animals.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is not needed because alternatives can cover the same outcomes
objection: Dissection teaches embodied, tactile, and variable real-tissue interpretation that alternatives cannot deliver with the same fidelity, and many classroom specimens are already dead or byproducts, so the practice remains justified.

target: AG1's claim that classroom dissection usually does not rely on wild capture because specimens are already dead/byproducts
objection: That assumption is unreliable because roughly 99% of dissection animals are reportedly caught in the wild, and wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity, so the ethical problem remains.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is unnecessary because it is not required by standards or medical training
objection: Even if not literally required, dissection can still be part of legitimate education because it develops hands-on lab competency and scientific motivation, and schools commonly include such additional learning experiences.

target: AG1's educational justification for dissection
objection: AP Biology, NGSS, and medical-competence goals can all be met without animal dissection, and when an activity is not required it adds avoidable harm rather than essential educational value.

target: AG2's claim that 'not strictly required' makes dissection unjustified
objection: Dissection can still be a necessary route to practical biology skills and real anatomical interpretation, so the fact that it is not explicitly mandated by standards does not make it unjustified.

target: AG1's claim that educational worth is enough to justify dissection
objection: Something that is merely worthwhile but not necessary should not be allowed when it harms animals and the environment; optional enrichment does not justify avoidable harm.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives make dissection only optional enrichment
objection: The assumption that alternatives can replace the embodied, tactile lab competencies of real dissection is false, because those core procedural and interpretive skills are learned through manipulating real tissue under realistic conditions.

target: AG1's claim that supervision and opt-outs make dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Safeguards do not remove the upstream harms of obtaining specimens, and when high-quality alternatives exist, schools should not authorize avoidable animal harm simply because the activity feels more hands-on.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is merely optional enrichment and ethically unjustified
objection: Real dissection is not optional enrichment, because it is a necessary route to embodied lab skills and authentic anatomical interpretation; moreover, the typical classroom supply is already dead/byproduct specimens, so the practice can be ethically framed as productive use rather than harm.

target: AG1's claim that oversight and opt-outs solve the ethical problem
objection: Even with oversight and opt-outs, the underlying supply chain can still be harmful, and if most specimens are sourced through wild capture the environmental harm remains regardless of classroom safeguards.

target: AG2's claim that wild-capture harms are unavoidable in classroom dissection
objection: Typical school dissections can use already-dead or meat-industry byproduct specimens, so the biodiversity harms from wild capture are not an unavoidable feature of allowing supervised student dissection.

target: AG1's claim that schools can generally procure only already-dead/byproduct specimens
objection: Schools usually cannot verify or audit the full upstream origin of every specimen, so vendor contracts and procurement promises cannot reliably ensure that dissection animals were not taken from the wild.

target: AG2's claim that schools cannot generally control specimen sourcing
objection: Schools can direct demand toward established byproduct streams, require provenance documentation, and specify already-dead/byproduct-only procurement, so they can generally source dissections without relying on wild-caught animals.

target: AG1's claim that procurement rules can keep dissection specimens out of wild-capture supply chains
objection: In practice, schools need large and continuous volumes, byproduct supply can be insufficient, and vendors can fill shortfalls with wild-caught animals, so byproduct-only procurement cannot reliably eliminate upstream harms.

target: AG2's claim that large-scale classroom demand inevitably forces wild-capture sourcing
objection: Common specimen streams such as fetal pigs are stable meat-industry byproducts, and schools can enforce byproduct-only contracts with provenance documentation, so wild-capture is not an inherent consequence of classroom demand.

target: AG1's claim that schools can reliably enforce byproduct-only sourcing
objection: Schools lack the auditing power and supply control needed to guarantee that every lot is truly byproduct-only, and substitutions or mislabeling can still allow wild-captured animals into the supply chain.

target: AG2's claim that procurement cannot generally keep dissection specimens to already-dead/byproducts
objection: Schools can generally manage sourcing through procurement specifications, lot-level documentation, and byproduct-based supply chains, so they can often direct demand away from wild-caught animals.

target: AG1's claim that documentation and procurement specifications can reliably prove byproduct-only origin
objection: Lot documents are often just vendor declarations without independent audit, and because schools cannot fully verify upstream sourcing or prevent substitutions, wild-capture can still remain part of the supply chain.
